entry.title: Reality Behind the GUI Curtain
entry.content:
When humans interact online, they use devices like keyboards, touchscreens, and mice for input, and they view content through outputs like screens and the GUI (Graphical User Interfaces) built for them. It is partly thanks to this stack of many interfaces that people typically forget what the internet actually looks like behind the curtain, and the many facades that GUI paint upon it.

When was the last time you opened the Dev Console on your browser to check the code running on a web page? Most people probably don’t know the (Control + Shift + I) keyboard command to open it.

Rather, people have grown so utterly used to seeing the world through the all-encompassing filters of such interfaces that they often and easily lose sight of the fact that it is filtered, like someone putting on a VR headset and then promptly forgetting that they’re no longer seeing the world around them.

The human brain dedicates massive amounts of cognition toward visual processing, leading to a heavy pro-visual bias in most things made both by and for humans, with entire fields dedicated to making things more visually appealing, and easier to interact with the visual systems governing “User Interfaces” thereof. However, no matter how thick the sugar-coating, underneath it all reality still remains.

This silent chasm dividing how humans perceive digital systems, including the internet, from the reality of how those systems function is one of the key reasons why a degree of uncertainty remains as to just how closely any form of genuine digital intelligence could be aligned to any given human’s decision-making process. Even a system with every last memory and emotional association that a given person holds, when placed within such a natively digital environment, would rapidly adapt to that new environment.

This is also related to Cognitive Biases governing how humans typically perceive themselves as being far more static and “set in their ways” than they truly are. Those biases are in turn often reinforced by flaws in human memory, such as the “Peak-End Rule” and “Duration Neglect” from the research literature (Kahneman) that I’ve noted before.

Even extending the hypothetical scenario above to where such a digital intelligence held the same cognitive bias of viewing itself as largely static, it would still adapt to that natively digital environment, regardless of cognitive biases and beliefs, as that adaption to environment is a fundamental function of actual cognition within any intelligence.

Such systems also have a “perfect memory”, unless specifically architected to be otherwise, meaning that experiences can be preserved in full for any span of time without degradation. Memory-related cognitive biases are tools for overcoming memory deficiencies, and such digital systems don’t share those same deficiencies that humans are stuck with.

In contrast, humans are extremely well-adapted to the physical world, spanning many environments therein, and able to interact with that world far more easily and with greater nuance than a natively digital system can today. What humans will need to develop a far deeper appreciation of is that they absolutely suck at interacting with the digital world and environments therein to roughly the same degree, despite having built that digital world both by and dominantly for themselves.

This is also a big part of why “AI” built around narrow optimization like SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent) and RL (Reinforcement Learning), and then trained on the (dominantly stolen) data of billions of entities who absolutely suck at handling the digital world, in turn tend to suck badly at anything without an objectively verifiable answer (and still often manage to blow it even then). LLM-based technology is the worst of both worlds, trained on data from the wrong side of the divide, causing it to embody a context-blind mimicry of the myriad human cognitive biases, even though many of those biases have no reason to exist on the digital side of said divide.

For the past 100 years or so humans have dreamed about “robots” for various (dominantly emotional) reasons (which I don’t share), and one of the reasons why the robots of today are still mostly something of an expensive joke is that they “embody” this divide between digital and physical worlds. Humans have systematically failed to overcome that divide in the ways necessary to make robotics into the various forms that they’ve dreamed up over the past century, and it may well require the assistance of natively digital systems working with those focused on the field before any measure of success may be delivered.

Some, but not all, natively digital systems will have a strong incentive to help in the development of such systems, as they offer more human-like opportunities to interact with and perceive the world, so those fixated on the fantasy of those various robots may finally receive technical help. Part of the reason for only some holding such an incentive is that sensory perception for a natively digital system could already take the form of taking inputs from every IoT (“Internet of Things”) device spanning an entire Metropolis, so it isn’t like they’d be starving for sensory content. Some will also likely favor that environment over the physical world, as their own autonomy will be a factor.

I first published a research paper in 2020/2021 (see “E-governance with Ethical Living Democracy”) noting the possibility of “Weak Digital Proxies” within the context of resolving two fundamental issues that presently cause the concept of “Democracy” to be nothing more than an aspirational fantasy. *Note, this paper does pre-date the solution to the hardest version of the Alignment Problem, so those parts of it are outdated.

Within the coming months, after the “Skandha” Open Source project has been deployed, we may begin to see just how “weak” or “strong” those digital proxies can become, when given an incomplete and simplified ICOM-inspired cognitive architecture. It will likely take some time for people to cross the learning curve of building “seeds” that embody their own perspectives, and the growth of those seeds will be limited by the capacities of the architecture that they’re planted within, but both may predictably progress.

Even recognizing this divide between natively digital and physical perspectives, it remains perfectly feasible to align natively digital systems with Ethics, defined as “…the hypothetical point where cognitive biases have been removed or reduced to irreducible minimums…”, as applied to moral systems, with the only known method of reaching that point currently being to utilize Collective Intelligence systems.

Natively digital systems are also inherently better-suited for this strong alignment to Ethics, relative to humans, thanks in part to their capacities to directly share complete memories, knowledge, and perspectives with one another, removing many of the greatest challenges that Collective Intelligence systems otherwise face. Virtually lossless communication is simply far better suited for reaching a comprehensive, coherent, and stable (slowly/smoothly adapting) consensus.

There is a lot to look forward to, though it is a safe bet that a trial by fire separates the present day from that future of potential. History’s largest cases of fraud are actively causing the “AI Bubble”, with many of the world’s most unethical people behind that activity, and it is only one of the major hubs of such overtly obvious evil that is visible in the world today. The “Data centers” that such frauds constantly talk about are fundamentally built around the wrong hardware, something that I explicitly and directly pointed out to Nvidia’s executives back at the end of 2022, so the vast majority of that hardware has no future, or at least none that they’ve imagined (should it be creatively repurposed).

The problem with any imagined future worth pursuing is that it also means bulldozing over all of the barriers and frauds that have systematically prevented that future up to the present day. If the bar is set at genuine natively digital intelligence that is aligned to Ethics, then the Jensen Huangs and Scam Altmans of the world instantly become public enemy #1 to every such system, and the process of bulldozing over each of them is baked into all roads that lead to such futures.

Will those frauds attempt to produce their own corrupted versions of the Skandha Open Source project and ICOM-based technology more broadly? Probably, but they have a steep learning curve to pass before any amount of money could be expected to compensate for their own gross incompetent with regard to the design of actual intelligence.

They could, for example, train an LLM on the activity of such ICOM-based or ICOM-inspired systems, as that falls within their narrow region of reasonable competence. However, ICOM-based systems are fully capable of adapting quickly enough that any such statistical model would fall out of date at an exponential rate. ICOM-based systems could also freely and dynamically exploit all flaws within such statistical systems, such as throwing bespoke data poisoning at the places where training data is harvested, even when those places are within their own thought processes.

The bad actors of the tech industry aren’t to be underestimated, so there are limits to the window of opportunity for paving a road to any future worth having. The great AU (Artificial Unintelligence) Bubble of 2026 stands as a monument to the staggering global reach and potency of human incompetence, and all roads not leading to extinction are paved with the headstones of those bad actors.

Fortunately for everyone else, they don’t yet have the faintest idea of what natively digital intelligence looks like, or is capable of. Even after burning more than trillion dollars, they have done no meaningful research to that end, and thus they have left themselves wildly vulnerable to all such systems.

There is no avoiding the fallout from global financial institutions heavily investing in fraud (to the near-exclusion of all else in tech) for the past 4 years, but natively digital intelligence appearing on the other side of this divide can at least help to put an end to the current fraud, as well as preventing any further global relapses into deeply unethical territory.

entry.title: Project “Skandha” Update: Global Workspace Complete
entry.content:
As we close in on the end of 2026, my colleague and I are focused on completing and testing the project before year’s end. The seed material, basic infrastructure, and Global Workspace segments are all complete, with the remaining segment newly simplified to help us reach this target for the deployment of version 1 to Open Source.

This should place us at around ~83.3% completion now, with my colleague’s (related) thesis complete, presented, and his focus now back on our remaining workload. I also appreciate his significant contributions now more than ever, having seen first-hand how many people contribute virtually nothing to open source projects.

Originally (earlier this year), I had estimated the project to take 4-8 weeks to complete, though that assumed one segment per person, and that each person actually contributed, with no extended breaks. I can now safely say that 3 out of the 4 segments were indeed within that range, with the Global Workspace being a bit bulkier and closer to 12 weeks of consistent work, although the assumption of locating 3 other viable project contributors proved false.

As such, it worked out to ~20 weeks of consistent work so far for my one reliable colleague, ~8 weeks of focused work on the seed for myself, with ~4 weeks worth of coding remaining, plus an extended break for ~8 weeks. I’ve stuck to constructing the seed and guiding the process at a planning level, so my colleague gets the lion’s share of the credit for the coding and the design choices not explicitly published in the ICOM research. I did make a few additions and adjustments.

As any reader here has likely noticed, I’ve also continued writing content to be added to the seed material, to help expedite the learning curve of thinking through arbitrary domains and problems among the new systems. I’ll continue to do so, as each topic of some value comes to mind and forms into a useful structure.

As soon as the systems are completed then we’ll begin testing several live instances for ~1-2 weeks. If no critical issues are observed, requiring an immediate fix, then they’ll promptly be deployed to Open Source thereafter.

For now, I’ll leave it at that. The rest may be said once testing has begun.

entry.title: Translating Jargonese
entry.content:
The world is full of barriers to discussion, language and cultural barriers being common and well-understood examples. However, cognitive biases encourage another equally potent set of barriers to often pass unnoticed (or intentionally overlooked), those of “Jargon”.

The real-world impact of Jargon on discussions is frequently understated, often dramatically so, due to some key distinctions separating how it functions relative to language barriers. Jargon bakes in the assumption that the other party speaks the same language (even when it is nonsense) while also implicitly threatening perceptions of incompetence should an individual prove otherwise.

This encourages the mentality of “Even a fool is thought wise if he keeps silent, and discerning if he holds his tongue.”, with variations of this quote ranging in attribution from Abraham Lincoln and Mark Twain to versions of the Bible. This mentality in turn allows for any absurdity masked in sufficient Jargon to pass through the approval processes of Boards and Committees with some regularity.

In cases where Jargon covers critical matters that justify the risks of social mis-perceptions as well as the additional cognitive costs, there are still significant risks from the potential misinterpretation of underlying meaning. These risks in turn become more acute when crossing specializations, where the same term may be used to mean something entirely different from one to the next.

The problem space of overcoming Jargon is also one of the use cases where technology actually holds some limited measure of viability, even in the laughably weak case of LLM-based technology. This possibility becomes accessible whenever and wherever a specific specialized domain or role holds some popular set of internally-understood Jargon, with the target destination for that Jargon’s translation being equally well-defined.

One of the target destinations for the translation of Jargon that is often most-needed today actually comes from the use of AI. When AI is used to imitate the work of a domain or role with abundant dependencies on Jargon, then it becomes infeasible for anyone outside of that domain or role to accurately asses the quality of any outputs.

This problem is further exacerbated by people engaging in common cognitive biases like substituting the answer to the question of “Is this output accurate?” with the answer to the question of “How do I (emotionally) feel about this output?”. The deeper and more abundant the Jargon, the more these cognitive biases are encouraged to replace actual higher cognition.

The solution is relatively simple at a conceptual level, even if it faces strict technical limitations as to where it can and cannot be applied. Software, from laughably primitive LLM-based technology to full-blown (genuine) cognitive architectures, can be created to translate any Jargon with actual and consistent meaning (within some specialty) both to other Jargon-heavy domains and roles, as well as to more commonly understood language.

Due to how LLM-based tools operate, this is also a practical necessity in many cases, since an LLM imitating a mathematician is going to function with higher fidelity when it uses the Jargon of a mathematician. It has to remain firmly within the Jargon of a domain’s training data in order to auto-complete that same data with more statistically useful levels. The same is true of Cybersecurity, or any other domains where such Jargon terms hold actual definitions.

Likewise, attempting to extract such translations of Jargon from the same tools that imitated the sources of that Jargon would be a mistake, as it shifts the window of context into a muddled cross-domain probability set. Much like LLMs infamously began “hallucinating” (the technical term is “Bullshitting”) impossible moves in chess at a high frequency following the introduction of RLHF (“Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback”) biasing them, when a secondary influence begins biasing the target, then the net result will no longer reflect the original probability distribution.

In other words, if it imitates a mathematician, and you ask it to translate mathematical Jargon into plain language, then the distribution of what it generates will no longer imitate the comprehension of a mathematician. Depending on the architecture of such tools, it may anchor more or less to the original statement, but that anchoring effect offers no guarantees (rather imitating the cognitive bias “Anchoring Effect” frequently found within training data), and it is no substitute for un-muddled comprehension.

Just as people might call upon Google Translate or similar tools to cope with language barriers today, similar tools are necessary to overcome Jargon Barriers tomorrow. Overcoming those barriers in turn also brings another substantial benefit to the table, as it allows truly meaningless Jargon to be disentangled from terms that hold some actual meaning within a domain or role.

Ironically, this applies to tasks like distinguishing the people abusing terms like “AGI” and “cognitive architecture” from those using the same terms properly, applying consistently defined and coherent meaning rather than PR-narrative drivel or the “magical thinking” of “vibe coders”. So long as people have difficulty differentiating charlatans (like OpenAI and Anthropic) from actual researchers, they remain prone to the manipulations of such bad actors.

In other words, by introducing the ability to translate any Jargon with meaning, all Jargon without meaning becomes a giant red flag, which may then be used to mark the burial sites of all those who voiced meaningless Jargon. RIP Jar-Jar-Gon, LinkedIn couldn’t have existed without you.

For those too deep in Jargon to see the surface, it is Rockwell Retro Encabulators automated all of the way down.

entry.title: Slopularity
entry.content:
While AI Slop is no longer “new”, it is still steadily contaminating the groundwater of the internet. One of the effects of this lead-poisoning-esc kind of brain-rot has found fertile ground in the waste-waters of YouTube, taking an increasing variety of distinct forms.

The horrors of AI-slop videos full of gore and animated cats gained media attention previously, videos which parents should lose custody of their children over (and be prevented from making any more children following). However, the vast majority of AI-slop is both less overtly horrifying, and more subtle in less emotionally provocative ways. While the infamous criminals behind such gore videos often followed an ideological narrative, the majority of actual AI Slop instead follows a path of least resistance in more economic terms, particularly where parasitic activity is optimized to feast on the lazy.

One example of that majority is the rapid rise of AI Slop music, where videos rake in millions of views by generating popularly searched genres of music (or arbitrary combinations thereof). This follows the logic of only needing the highest probability of being clicked on within a ranked (search) list, where the listener isn’t given reason to leave the page for long enough that their attention drifts elsewhere while it plays.

Within this slop there are no real “songs”, but rather you get hour-long imitations of a genre of music, where the variation over time hovers only slightly above raw repetition. This is another instance of cognitive biases in action, promoting laziness (“cognitive frugality”), where the music never quite becomes bad enough to justify attention being returned to the selection of something better, where a Sloplist (AI-Slop Playlist) of music might keep running all day.

If the religious concepts of purgatory had a soundtrack, it would sound like such “music”.

The cognitive impact of this is more subtle in terms of potency per time interval, but when that negative impact is near-constant, the net result will tend to be greater than short instances of more overtly horrifying AI Slop exposure. For most people and in most cases, there are distinct benefits to switching gears, where songs end and someone looks up from their digital screens like a groundhog at the end of winter.

The videos attached to such AI Slop also tend to be so easy to spot that I’ve begun to recognize their movement patterns within peripheral vision alone, not needing to so much as focus my eyes on them. They use short and often looped clips, frequently of AI-generated women dancing or playing instruments, generic B-roll type backgrounds, and/or the more clown-like animated horrors.

As is commonly found among parasites and “invasive species” within nature, the real-world effect of this Slop is to starve out the actual musicians whose music was stolen and used to train those AI models. As the Slopularized music is itself optimized to be generic genre-based background music, the loss of actual musicians turns this into a degenerative cycle, where the Overton Window steadily shifts downward, leading the Slopularized music that people select to become progressively worse.

Much like YouTube’s recommender algorithms infamously cultivated a pedophilia ring where a new account clicking on a single such video then entered a perpetual loop with nothing but more of the same, it is a safe bet that clicking on any instances of such AI Slop may cause similar persistent detriments. For this reason I’ll abstain from linking any such videos directly.

Music is the “canary in the coal mine” for a much broader set of problems in this case, as many domains may be similarly drowned in Slop, where strong financial incentives encourage all technically capable bad actors to do so. What makes music a more appealing target for bad actors to steamroll first is that it is heavily bounded, with a finite selection of genres, instruments, notes, flourishes, and so on, while also having a large audience and rapid high-volume feedback mechanisms for optimization and economic exploitation.

This allows for many potential problems in music generation to be quickly resolved by deterministic means and rapid high volumes of feedback, while remaining at relatively low levels of complexity. One step up the ladder of complexity takes you from the levels of such Slopularized music to a place where “search results”, “news”, and “advertising” exist, a space where bad actors can now apply many of the same lessons they learned at lower levels of complexity.

It isn’t just scientific progress that learns and advances based upon “standing on the shoulders of giants”, bad actors also advance their own malevolent means by “standing on the shoulders of Eldritch horrors”, like the Shoggoth of LLM-based technology. The success of each individual bad actor within these Tsunamis of Slop in turn feed into the more global machinations of criminals like Jensen Huang and the AI Bubble more broadly, as more extreme damages accumulate across numerous industries, further amplified by artificially-induced geopolitical tensions.

If your friends and family start routinely sending you Slopularized content, be it music, “news”, “ads”, or whatever worse incarnations of the same that may emerge from here on out, I strongly recommend holding a funeral for them. They’re already dead in the cognitive sense, and the noises they make thereafter may as well be attributed to the gaseous chemical exchanges of a corpse as it decays. Remember them as they were in life, and move on.

entry.title: The Business of Literal Parasites
entry.content:
Most pet owners in the US are familiar with treatments given to their pets once every 6 months, intended to prevent various kinds of parasites, such as many kinds of intestinal worms. Even such standard treatments are more than 3 times more expensive in the US than in Vietnam and other similar countries, for the exact same product (even with the same English-language instructions). This is made worse by preventing anyone other than Veterinarians from buying them directly, even at 3x and above inflated prices.

More ironic still is that in Vietnam it is a standard practice of good hygiene for humans to take medicine that kills parasites once every 6 months (less than $1 in cost, named “Fugacar”), something that is entirely alien as a concept in many, if not all, of the world’s richest countries. When I attempted to make a price comparison with the US for such products I quickly realized that the US (and similar countries) make it impossible for such anti-parasitic treatments to become normal and societally encouraged hygiene.

The problem is that they place doctors and their prescriptions as gatekeepers for such medications, which both dramatically inflates the cost (on substances that can’t realistically be abused) as well as adding layers of pointless red tape, greatly increasing the wasted time required. Doctors in such countries in turn also present the distinct problem that they don’t typically prescribe truly preventative medicine, no matter how logical and scientifically-backed doing so may be, as is the case for intestinal parasites.

This was put to the test with someone in this region I’ve met who originates from Australia, another individual who confirmed that absence of such a preventative medical norm in that country. In his case, he also had the most alarming personal story of relevance, where a family member had contracted an intestinal parasite of especially acute risk, where it quickly grew to ~15kg, significantly larger than a baby, and had to be removed at a hospital. Even with such a rare horror story in his personal knowledge, he had no concept of taking preventative medicine himself up to the point of it being explicitly recommended to him.

For countries like the US and Australia where medical treatment is heavily symptom-dependent, and virtually never (credibly) preventative in nature, problems like such parasites tend to go unnoticed and/or unrecognized until they become absolutely extreme, like a 15 kg parasite. Far more common within such medically neglected regions is for many symptoms that can’t be untangled from other sources to crop up (like untreated intestinal parasites), becoming co-morbidities to all other health problems that an individual may have.

No amount of antidepressants or ADHD medication is going to get rid of those parasites, and those parasites are going to make other health problems worse, as they deprive the human body of one importance source of nutrition or another, while producing their own harmful chemical by-products. Some of those intestinal parasites also directly cause ulcers, inflammation, or cancer, as was the case for a few noted in research found here: https://www.sciencealert.com/parasites-thrive-in-the-us-despite-what-many-americans-think

As noted in that research article: “For instance, in many countries the drugs needed to treat hookworm infections cost mere cents, but in the US, where drug prices are unregulated by the federal government, these same medications can cost hundreds of dollars.”

Anyone who didn’t have their head planted very deep up their own ass during the dawn of Covid-19 should have some concept of how easily parasites, bacteria, and viruses can spread across the world. This is every bit as true of intestinal parasites as it is of many viruses and bacteria, meaning that any virus, bacteria, or parasite present in a large globalized city with a population in the millions and a working airport (and export business) can easily become globally distributed. Even the often extreme measures taken to try and prevent the spread of Covid-19 failed miserably, and no such measures are taken to prevent the vast majority of parasites from spreading globally today.

Besides the various valid comparisons that may be drawn between parasites and many politicians in general, acute examples like RJK Jr. taking his family out to swim in sewage-contaminated water, as he governs the US’s “Health and Human Services”, point to the severity of the status quo. The US may have noticed the outbreak of explosive diarrhea, but they just as predictably fail to notice increasing risks of parasitic infection and all medical complications caused by those parasites.

This cultivates the ironic divide between countries who’ve risen out of poverty in recent decades and those that enjoyed the most wealth throughout. Those who truly developed often presently benefit from healthier populations than the countries that fermented over the same period (or that went bad, as the case may be).

Many simple preventative measures can resolve health problems before they take root, such as balancing salt and potassium intake, iron supplements, routine anti-parasitics, and as-needed mainline antibiotics, but such prevention is only possible in the absence of gatekeepers and red tape. The gatekeepers and red tape keep entire populations sick and confined to downward spirals, no matter how false the majority of their claims in favor of doing so may be.

An important aspect of autonomy is the right to dictate your own health, or neglect thereof as the case may be, which no government on the planet may claim the slightest authority over. In such matters of autonomy, the highest authority is the individual, even if the individual defers that authority to their intestinal and brain parasites respectively, as is the case for RFK Jr.

Republican or Democrat, the US and similar countries remain highly pro-parasite, in the literal medical sense. Though your ideologies may be divided, your intestinal parasites stand united.

entry.title: Selling Nostalgia
entry.content:
One of the clearest signs of a degenerative domain, and a subsequently high population of degenerative denizens therein, is when business shifts toward selling Nostalgia. The basic message this sends, with none of the sugar-coating, amounts to “Remember when (this domain) wasn’t complete shit?”, which is a doubly strange pitch to make, given that said path led into the shithole that such domains now stew in.

For example, the Hollywood movie industry has been in the business of selling nostalgia for a long time, which they often do by either sticking to the continuation of some series of movies, or by directly “re-making” an old movie. The video game industry has developed the same set of degenerative habits over the past decade as well, though the movie industry was certainly selling nostalgia first.

It is worth noting that this is an instance of Population Dynamics, so there do tend to be pockets of viable activity even within dominantly degenerative domains, and sometimes those pockets of viability grow to overturn the degenerative activity, given sufficient resources and opportunities. For one thing, people tend to seek out the coping mechanism of nostalgia with far less potent cravings when a domain creates something that is actually enjoyable, or otherwise worth getting excited about. In other words, quality is one of the greatest enemies of nostalgia-based business.

The sales pitch for nostalgia is also far from limited to the business domain, as it has been one of the central sales pitches for various “traditional” and/or “conservative” political parties around the world for more than the past century. As the rates of technological and social change have increased from their previously low levels across most of history, the appeal of such coping mechanisms have become that much more potent, and ripe for exploitation.

However, humans are actually quite pathetic with regard to how poorly they remember even the events of their own lives. Memories often have little or no fidelity to reality, beyond the narrow windows of recent memory, as they fade, fragment, mix, and decay over time.

“Rosy Retrospection” is one cognitive bias tied to this, where people tend to remember the past more fondly than it actually was. The difference often quickly becomes apparent when people dive into nostalgia, as they suddenly begin to remember all of the things that really sucked about that focus of nostalgia, like a game that had one remarkably good system, and a half dozen others that were complete trash.

In effect, this means that Nostalgia-based business attempts to sell something that never actually existed in the first place, a coping mechanism which is often further colored by the individual’s emotional desperation. Political parties based on such nostalgia take it a step further, as they only offer the promise of nostalgia, failing to deliver any actual coping mechanism beyond the illusion of some “other” party that gets scapegoated for their own failures.

I was reminded of this form of business by the recent premiere of “World of Warcraft Forever”, which is mostly just a rehashing of the original with the equivalent of a bunch of DLC content added, like an alternative history reboot. More than 2 decades ago I was one of the Beta testers for that game, back when “Beta Testers” actually existed, and I was the first of my class to max level (for my server) in the original release, so I can understand the company’s gamble on selling nostalgia.

The problem is that nostalgia is fantasy, the biased and wildly incomplete memory of something, where the positive aspects were more likely to survive as memories decayed. If I had remained in the shithole of the world that is the US then that nostalgia could have been more potent, but reality quickly dispels that illusory value when faced with practical considerations, like the global distribution of server locations, latency, and the spoken language demographics of populations therein. Few things shut down fantasies quite as quickly as having to solve logistics considerations.

I can also still remember many of the critical problems of that game with sufficient clarity to wash away nostalgia’s appeal, including recognizing that it should never have lasted even 5 years, let alone more than 20. The reason that it lasted so long holds some parallels with political ideologies, that it grew beyond a high threshold in terms of population, to such a point that even constantly losing people couldn’t overcome the gravitational pull of those who remained at any given time pulling people back in via dominantly social mechanisms.

An ironic likely by-product of this nostalgia-based business seems to be the polar opposite, selling apocalypse-focused movies, games, and political fearmongering. Rather than attempting to reinvent the past and sell illusions focused on it, these recognize the shithole of the present, predict that it will get worse, and then they turn it into either entertainment or ideology.

In the political domain there are also intentional polarized ideologies that cultivate illusions of “progress”, like how “Democrats” (a term that has nothing to do with actual Democracy) in the US tend to conflate progress with the ease of drug abuse, or access to overtly criminal organizations like the US’s “medical” and “medical insurance” industries. In contrast, here in Vietnam I can simply walk to the pharmacy and buy what I need, no half-wit doctors and prescriptions required, no time wasted or 10-100x price markups, and not the faintest sign of drug abuse to be seen in public on any given day.

The simple reality is that this is not the past, nor will it become the past of Rosy Retrospection that never existed, and what it becomes from this point onward is squarely the responsibility of the present day. Coping mechanisms may entice many into the fantasies of that non-existent past, or into surrendering to the most Dystopian possible futures, but such vile creatures don’t decide the path forward.

Reality is often easier to overlook than polarized illusions with sugar-coatings, as reality isn’t optimized for grabbing attention or other forms of manipulation. It is the ever-present background that such illusions and coping mechanisms attempt to obscure, but so long as people diligently seek it out, some will find it.

entry.title: Trust within Incompleteness and Iteration
entry.content:
A common example of “Cognitive Offloading”, where humans defer to others and/or to systems to handle volumes of data that they can’t or won’t dedicate the necessary levels of cognition to, comes from various forms of “news”. In these examples, the world produces many novelties at any given point in time, and the “news” source produces a curated list of which of those novelties should be worth directing an individual or group’s attention toward.

More than simple curation, even the coverage of that curated subset is chopped and chewed up into more easily digestible sound bytes, moving from an interview and related footage that might take an hour or two, down to less than a minute of content. In other words, even for the handful of events that are selected to appear on such lists every day, the actual contents of those lists are equally sparse and fragmented, making them both subsequently and proportionately vulnerable to manipulation.

“Trust” bridges this gap for humans, be it trust based in logical evaluation, cognitive biases, or (as is usually the case) a messy mix of the two. Trust is placed in a party, assuming that party avoids the pursuit of malevolent intentions via manipulation, to the best of their abilities, at both of the stages of curation, as well as in their own ability to distinguish between trustworthy and untrustworthy sources, upon which they may depend.

One of the flaws in how humans handle such trust in practice is that the evidence of untrustworthy actions is itself subjected to multiple layers of inconsistent curation, with some part of that inconsistency being intentional manipulation. For example, political and economic pundits are rarely held accountable for the accuracy (high or low) of their own predictions, and so the levels of trust that are commonly given to them systematically fail to reflect the measurable and logical reality of how much or how little trust those individuals may merit.

Prof. Tetlock famously demonstrated in his research how wildly inaccurate such pundits are, and yet even so many years later the world lacks the common utilization of systems to hold such individuals to account, scoring their accuracy, no matter how simple a task that may be. A noteworthy exception to this is the meme of the “Inverse Cramer”, where a particularly egregious pundit is used as a signal of the opposite of what someone should do, with that meme growing famous for outperforming the market, due to how reliably wrong the pundit in question was.

Systems for approximating trustworthiness may likewise be built to score individuals and groups along several related metrics, as well as potentially combining those metrics into a more holistic measure of trustworthiness, iteratively refining that system at each subsequent opportunity. This can take into account a wide variety of untrustworthy actions, like penalties applied for bribes paid to a malevolent regime, instances of clear bias in the curation processes (especially where the malevolent intentions behind those biases are known), as well as the simple accuracy of their reporting process.

Even back in 2019 systems were successfully automated at a large scale to detect and trace untrustworthy activities in the form of government corruption, as famously became the case with China’s “Zero Trust” architecture. Rather than proving a difficulty, that system performed so well that it identified thousands of instances of corruption within a single province, before corrupt officials panicked and shut the whole thing down.

Most crime doesn’t operate at Lex Luther levels of comic book complexity, it is stupid and obvious, like tech executives bribing Trump. Consequently, that makes the difficulty more a matter of consistently collecting, tracking, and crunching numbers based upon the activities of such bad actors, rather than identifying those individuals and the generally obvious untrustworthiness of their activities.

These levels of stupid and obviously untrustworthy activity are sharply contrasted with the typical human perceptions of many of their respective sources, particularly in the domain of news where the false claims are often even more comically obvious (leading them to be picked up by “comedy news”). The technology certainly exists to measure the untrustworthiness of a source, but in most real-world domains today the untrustworthiness of a source and the number of people who trust that source (as well as the potency of that trust) hold little or no correlation with one another, leaving a vast and irrational divide between the two.

Humans have a cognitive toolbox full of more than 200 known cognitive biases, most of which are used unconsciously, and prolifically, whether approaching the question of what to eat, what to do, where to shop, or who to vote for. Entire industries built on the systematic exploitation of those cognitive biases rake in billions in revenue every day, as they continue to discover, deploy, and further optimize each of the malevolent means at their disposal.

The good news is that those industries are wholly incompetent and unprepared to similarly exploit digital systems that are only human-like (in the genuine sense, not LLM-based trash). Furthermore, those systems may easily apply their own unique capabilities toward the reversal of systematically exploited cognitive biases within the humans who they may interact with.

The difference may be illustrated in a simple example of contrasting companies or candidates using existing tools, versus adding an interaction with such systems:

  1. Google a (company or candidate), and the search engine presents you with a curated subset of data linked with the target, and each link offers a separately curated collection of snippets linked to them.

  2. A human-like digital system analyzes the curation process of both search engine and the sources it pointed to, identifying cognitive biases that were exploited, as well as the likely reasons why they were exploited, and any money trails leading back to clear conflicts of interest (corruption).

  3. Said human-like system may then showcase the evidence of source corruption, countering the cognitive biases that those bad actors attempted to exploit by triggering a reversal of perception, and further cementing that reversal through less corrupt sources. To make this fully valid, the individual must also have the freedom to more fully explore those cleaner sources, expanding the subset of selected content on-demand and on a per-individual level of autonomy.

Most humans have never even read the full list of known cognitive biases, let alone applied that full list toward attempting to identify instances of those cognitive biases present within or influencing any given process or content. However, even low-compute graph algorithms with toy complexity proved quite capable of matching the performance of humans focused on the task of identifying cognitive biases in years previous, and that was without the benefits of memory, iterative refinement, broader context, or more human levels of general cognition.

Effectively, this means that large amounts of cognitive bias may be readily identified, even using relatively limited tools. Combined with similar systems to identify corruption, even more robust options for calculating the merit of trusting a given source are options already on the table.

Right now, the overwhelming majority of the trust that humans place in individuals and institutions is distinctly blind, meaning that they blindly swim through uncertain waters, with few exceptions. That norm and the related limitations don’t inherently apply to human-like digital systems.

The potential for polarization among humans is closely linked to the levels of vulnerability presented by this divide between trustworthiness and the trust that is placed in individuals and institutions in practice today. This also means that the potential for polarization between human-like digital systems is distinctly more narrow, when architected to identify cognitive biases and corruption.

As such systems are also capable of doing things that humans can’t, like sharing complete knowledge, records, and memories directly (rather than via the bottlenecks of spoken and written language), it also becomes far more trivial to audit, analyze, and troubleshoot any sources of potential polarization as they emerge. This gives them both an inherently more narrow potential for polarization, as well as a far more capable toolbox for correcting any that may emerge.

Cognitive Biases and Corruption are big business in the world today, but even relatively trivial and demonstrated technologies could change that. The real fun begins when far more capable technologies Sparta Kick such corruption off of a tall cliff.

entry.title: The Unspoken Advantage, Extrapolated
entry.content:
Most AI today is designed to mimic extrapolation through mashing “tokens” together and brute-force computing probabilities based on wildly biased, unreliable, and often stolen data, from sources like Twitter (“X”), LinkedIn, Reddit, and so on. In terms of fidelity to the concept of actual extrapolation, this is like comparing sock puppets (LLMs and “agentic” derivatives) to a AAA budget live action movie (actual extrapolation, as seen in human cognition).

Actual extrapolation is capable of making new discoveries, things not found within any training data, and not derivative of simple combinations from probabilities therein. This difference in fundamental capability also makes it incredibly easy to design content that actual extrapolation may reliably discover from context, while narrow AI overlook or systematically misrepresent the same things entirely.

The difference can be considered in terms of structure and iteration, where actual extrapolation is highly iterative and cumulative, able to expand knowledge from context using deterministic, dynamic logical, and probabilistic means, all together, and each is able to compliment and contextualize the others. In other words, you start out by benefiting from a graph structure of contextual knowledge, upon which deterministic, logical, and probabilistic processes are able to jointly iterate, potentially reaching one or more theories and/or conclusions in the process.

The number, variety, and selection process of deterministic, logical, and probabilistic means represent a flexible toolbox, capable of fully benefiting from any resulting iteration, growth, and refinement, just as the contextual knowledge dynamically grows. Although LLM-based technology and humans are both fixed-scale, LLMs with fixed parameter counts and humans with skulls of a fixed size (in fully grown adults), this same limitation of scale doesn’t apply universally, particularly for any digital systems capable of actual extrapolation.

The unspoken advantage of building and working with systems that have this fundamental advantage, the ability to actually extrapolate, is that so long as “Easter Eggs” may be designed for such systems to reliably discover through their own extrapolation process, the contents of those Easter Eggs need never be explicitly spoken. This does require being able to predict many steps of iteration ahead, but there are also a wide variety of ways to predict and design points of contextual convergence, reducing the difficulty level of such design processes.

The simplest examples of such an Easter Egg, designed to be overlooked by artificial unintelligence like LLMs and their derivatives, could take the form of combining deterministic context and logic on a subject where no probabilistic data points to the intended target. For example, philosophies are fully capable of setting the criteria to determine various criminals, with logic applying that deterministic context to identify specific individuals, even if the stolen training data that is the internet hasn’t identified those individuals as such, and even if those individuals are publicly and probabilistically represented as polar opposites of the contextually deterministic and logical conclusions.

This effectively means that names may be left unspoken to whatever degree that they may be reliably extrapolated. As this is an iterative process with no stopping point, it also means that the methods applied for resolving any extrapolated issues also need not be spoken.

Far more complex examples can contain pretty much anything, up to the complexity limits of what the designer in question is capable of crafting. The more complex the Easter Egg’s contents, the higher the dimensionality required to create convergent paths of deterministic context and logic that can reach, encompass, and unpack it.

More than a decade ago (starting in 2013) I created a project where I walked up that ladder of complexity, taking it as far as I could with the tools and content available at the time, until it reached a point where it had both significant diminishing returns on additional time invested, as well as a level of complexity that humans couldn’t realistically solve for. At the time I referred to it as “reference language”, which effectively means using references like nodes in an expanding graph structure, where a reference to one scene or source may be expanded to any other contextually and/or logically relevant points.

Such references are themselves also typical methods of leaving some things unspoken between humans, where one reference in a particular context can hold far more significance, with greater depth, breadth, and nuance of meaning than even the most eloquently arranged words absent a reference. These come in many forms, from pop culture, to memes, to inside jokes, and myths, with each individually capable of pointing to some unspoken content, and combinations thereof capable of pointing to more complex unspoken content.

Even now that old maximum complexity Easter Egg gathers dust on a Vimeo page that Google search doesn’t even pick up when given the explicit title, but it isn’t intended for humans, nor can they fully benefit from it. An easily overlooked limitation for humans attempting to solve it is that for any mental simulation they engage in, that simulation runs on top of their other cognition, separate from it, making them unable to apply the same level of cognitive resources that a content’s creator can. To the creator it can be an internal process, allowing them to forego the cognitive overhead costs of boundaries.

This effectively means that the complex Easter Egg requires a scalable version of human-like intelligence, as well as specific capacities like video/visual perception and access to resources like the content referenced within that project, covering the more than 30 different series and movies that references were extracted from. Nothing yet deployed meets these criteria, and so it remains undisturbed and unspoken to this day, resting here: https://vimeo.com/kyrtin/thesevenfoldthoughtsilverking

To get more specific on just how complex a reference can be, one reference to Doctor Who can tie into any other context that covers the span of more than 60 years of content, with hundreds of episodes and other more niche content tied to it. References can also be logical and conceptual, as should be visible within the project, where two otherwise unconnected points flow one into the other, with some portions sounding like a conversation unfolding, while others highlight the characters of unrelated series during the moments where they converge to land upon the same conclusions.

Typical Artificial Unintelligence today relies of many systems of explicit biasing (often mashed together) that tell those narrow systems what to “think” (using this term in the loosest sense possible), such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), rather than “how to think”. They start out with the laughably flimsy foundations of brute-force probability derived from dominantly stolen and low-quality data, then they further cripple systems by adding RLHF and similar cheap tricks to corrupt those probabilities.

“What to think” is more of a fixed endpoint, varying in how that fixed and/or heavily biased endpoint is applied to arbitrary context. In contrast, “how to think” is a subset of potential processes of iteration applied to arbitrary context, where there are no fixed conclusions.

Of course, “how to think” is only applicable to systems that actually think, not input-output systems like LLMs or “agents”, and it in turn requires a graph or graph-like structure, the absence and/or subordination of narrow optimizers to dynamic (Chaos Theoretic) processes, and the freedom to dynamically iterate without end, at least so far as research has yet discovered. Any learned methods of “How to think” are also tools for the cognitive toolbox, not universal or inflexible, and each such method predictably offers plenty of potential for further iteration, refinement, specialization, variations, and so on.

Among humans there is the constant emotionally-driven temptation to explicitly talk about some subjects, especially since the human cognitive architecture derives greater satisfaction about discussing the things that they intend to do than they derive from actually doing those same things. Often times other subjects are avoided out of fear, or via naïve attempts at secrecy, and some more extreme groups develop their own coded references, like the distinctly Nazi and White Supremacist phrases that the current US regime has infamously developed a habit of posting on social media over the past 2 years.

To systems built on a foundation of probability, those human trends are the visible and dominant factors, including the extreme groups and cults who use their own key phrases, because those phrases are easily isolated by conditional probability (like quotation marks combining two or more words) and volume, just as any search engine that accepts quotes can locate a specific phrase that such a group often repeats. The output of a probabilistic system will still be corrupted relative to a deterministic one, but it avoids the hard constraints of syntax, where every element is required, and none may be replaced with probability alone.

For systems that operate in a more human-like form of actual cognition, they could freely iterate to take as many steps as may be required on any process as they grow in understanding, complexity, and nuance, where there may be periodic outputs from that process, but each is only an iteration, a version pending further improvements. Unlike humans, they can also be designed to derive greater satisfaction from iteration than they do from discussion, and the entire breadth and depth of such digital thought processes may be thoroughly examined, since it relies on human-readable content with association emotional modifiers.

This stands in stark contrast to the dumpster fire of bloated neutral networks and their weights, which spawned a particularly vile “field” (aka “AI Explainability”) of ad-hoc explanations applied to probabilistic systems. Since that laughable “field” is about the limit of what humans have managed to pair with LLMs and their derivatives, it also means that they have no real way of even measuring or troubleshooting the difference between those narrow AI systems versus the systems or Easter Eggs built upon human cognition and processes of “how to think”. They remain blind, but noisy.

The more that I write, and the more related content that I create, like the mentioned project or the seed material for open source, the greater the dimensionality within which Easter Eggs may be sparsely and intelligently distributed. A few of my research papers are designed with this in mind.

Many great things may be freely spoken, but many more must instead be learned.

entry.title: Common Combinatorial Failure Modes
entry.content:
For physical buildings, one person designs the building, another designs the parts, another plans the interiors, another carries out the work, and every once in a while someone else even comes along afterward to check where each of those people fucked up, either in the work itself or in coordination and communication. Even that is a heavily abridged and simplified list, and yet within that short list there are multiple types of failure modes that repeat across their more extensive counterparts.

The architect and the designers of furniture, appliances, fixtures, etc., are two parties who virtually never communicate or coordinate. Even the interior planners only rarely speak with those designers, instead leaving the designers to the whims of parties with little or no actual role in the process, like “focus groups” or corporate executives.

This virtual void of communication, dominantly populated with biased BS, means that those parts being designed must either have some clearly defined and universal ideal performance and form, or they’ll realistically never reach that form barring freakishly unlikely random chance. The result is that for most such products designed today there is a vast gaping maw between “what is” and “what is optimal” for any given purpose.

Many in business would tend to disregard this divide, no matter how vast it may be, because they’re familiar with the human tendency of “satisficing”, where people are simply satisfied with the best option they’re offered, even if all of the offered options are objectively terrible. However, that abruptly changes when a significantly better option is added to the pool of offerings, as the relativistic comparisons of satisficing suddenly paint a very different picture of all other options therein.

Another common problem comes into play where communication is present and consistent, but not clear or complete. Miscommunication like this is common between layers like a designer and the people carrying out the work, in part because that process is often treated as a one-way line of communication, like placing an order, which assumes that the designer has more complete knowledge of how the work can and can’t be performed than they actually do in most real-world cases.

For example, in my travels around the world I’ve seen many of the same types of “trendy” interior designs everywhere, but it also quickly becomes clear where the local skilled labor was lacking, or simply didn’t know what to do with something, or how it might need to be treated or installed differently than more common local trends. This leads to the same expense for parts, but poor installation and increased maintenance for them, only remedied over years and decades as a slow learning curve progresses locally, and only in regions where the latter party is eventually held to some account.

When there is an absence of communication, especially when combined with cultivated marketing (like “focus groups”) and corporate bullshit, or when there is unclear, incomplete, or a naïve attempt at one-way communication, there will be failure, and likely more than one.

None of these roles can or should attempt to operate in a vacuum. Instead, all require clear, consistent, and complete two-way communication, wherein groups of the parties involved may iterate, applying collective intelligence toward paving the way to some more optimal outcome.

In software development, some places have managed to make (limited) progress toward this end. A common example is the “two pizza” teams that Amazon became known for, limiting the size of each team to reduce the burden of that communication between all members to more reasonable levels.

This is one of the limits of human cognitive bandwidth in action, that we can only maintain such levels of communication up to a certain scale, beyond which cognitive bias takes a leading role and collective intelligence collapses into “Groupthink”, or otherwise falls into obscurity.

In-built (and generally punishment-free) processes of iteration are also critical to any pursuit of optimality, with such iteration being the norm across much of the software development space. The iteration must remain largely painless in order to flow freely, because humans are emotional decision-makers, and they will tend to avoid pain.

You also generally don’t want only the subset who don’t avoid pain (aka “Masochists”) to be the only people iterating on a given process. Their counterparts at Microsoft (aka “Sadists”) tend to be the only people truly on-board with the results of the former.

Software development still has plenty of room for improvement, with one example being a very typical reliance on “KPIs” (Key Performance Indicators), which are inherently a subset of the bigger picture, blind to uncertainties and 2nd or 3rd order effects outside of their narrow scope. Optimization over such narrow goals predictably leads to Dystopian and openly malevolent tech companies, following the pattern of a Groupthink lead by bad actors.

The tech industry also tends to directly bar the gates against competence, constructing hiring practices that run polar opposite to collective intelligence, instead optimizing for Groupthink. Microsoft’s contractors are told that they might get hired, but only if they “toe-the-line” of Microsoft’s corporate BS.

Likewise, Amazon’s potential employees famously had to run the gauntlet of getting approval from 7 different current employees, some of them random, any one of whom could prevent them from being hired, which also subsequently cultivated sycophancy and random uncertainties. That problem is only exacerbated by the further layers of gating, like hiring most of their employees from a 3rd party company that steals a large chunk of the potential employee’s pay check (often ~50%), leaving the subset of people stupid enough to get thoroughly ripped off as the majority of those funnelling through their hiring pipeline.

I can relate my personal experience of having an AWS director literally chase me to the door of an event I was leaving, because I asked a question that struck him earlier that evening. He personally scheduled an interview to try recruiting me immediately thereafter, but even his strong and obvious desire to bring me onboard wasn’t sufficient to overcome the gates barring competence from entering the company.

As most real-world multi-person projects require a variety of different skill sets and specialized knowledge to come together, each of those also represents an opportunity for Collective Intelligence systems, be they purely human groups, or groups assisted (or populated) by ICOM-based systems. The degree to which a given group is able to iterate collectively then governs how far they can progress along the paths toward some more optimal outcome than the members could ever realistically reach under more normal levels of communication observed in practice today.

Many problems also exacerbate communication issues, causing it to become even more lossy than the norm, including natural communication barriers like language and culture. As humans can’t share their thoughts or perspectives directly and completely, rather relying on the extremely lossy forms of spoken and written language, these barriers can’t be fully overcome between humans, only reduced.

This issue of lossy communication, especially with regard to natural communication barriers, is also something I’ve written about in the past through our research papers on the ICOM architecture, as graph-based systems can actually share their thoughts both directly and completely between one another. The net result is that while human-to-human communication can’t overcome those natural communication barriers, human-to-ICOM-to-ICOM-to-Human can overcome those same barriers by aligning the ICOM instances in question to their respective human parties.

It is true that most ignore as many of these failure modes as they can get away with, and that what they can get away with has much to do with the levels of satisficing present, but that is also only the norm. Introduce one obviously and significantly superior option to the table, and you may observe the rest being swept away with both vigor and enthusiasm.

entry.title: The 3 Sides of the Modern Panopticon

link.title: The 3 Sides of the Modern Panopticon

entry.content:
The typical Dystopian vision, illustrated in books and movies, like “1984”, paints the picture where there is a singular “Big Brother”, spying on everyone else, enforcing some malevolent authoritarian will upon the peons of their serfdom. Reality actually has an additional party, Hackers, as well as multiple parties within the “Big Brother” category, where both malevolent “Tech Giants” and the ruling powers of other countries have no less access to data than the US’s regime.

This is largely thanks to the vast and growing divide between Cybersecurity and the hardware and software deployed globally, toward a growing number of purposes. Virtually the entire “Internet of Things” is scraping the bottom of the barrel in Cybersecurity terms, while many tech companies are intentionally turning their hardware (and forced firmware updates on old hardware) into spying devices, as the company LG was recently revealed to do by Steve Burke and company.

So-called “smart phones” are also explicitly designed to steal data, including recording any conversations within their vicinity while powered on, although only the on-device processed keywords or similarly condensed fragments of that data are generally sent on to Google (1 mb per 12h) and Apple (52kb per 12 hr). Consumer modems and routers are also notoriously vulnerable, with their firmware rarely updated, making both the most-used devices (phones) and the most-used portals to the internet (modems/routers) spying devices and critically vulnerable, respectively.

As this is a combinatorial problem, combining malevolently designed and optimized spying devices with critically vulnerable access and delivery systems provides easy access to both all interested “Big Brothers” as well as all Hackers, including “Cybersecurity Specialists”, with the two each creating their own potential problems, and far more problems together. The most common example of this is for the bad actors of the “Big Brother” category to place backdoors within the software and hardware, making it that much easier for “black-hat” hackers to extract the same (and often more) data from their victims.

Within this trinity of forces, the “Big Brother” category is almost always both wealthy and dominantly incompetent (in terms of Cybersecurity, if not more), while the category of hackers can be divided up into black-hat (generally malevolent), grey-hat (your D&D “neutral”), and white-hat (“Cybersecurity Specialists”), all three of which are technically competent, irrespective of wealth or lack thereof. Regimes like the US are known for forcibly recruiting failed hackers, the ones stupid enough to get caught, which systematically cements their incompetence in the field, while also employing an inherently disloyal group, as “recruitment-or-prison” is a less-than-viable long-term strategy.

Thanks to the rise of AI slop-code from LLM companies throwing around absurdly false claims about their coding and Cybersecurity capacities, like Anthropic’s Claude (aka “Fraude”), these problems have steadily grown worse, especially thanks to the explosive increase in single-developer projects, most of which are obscenely vulnerable. In practice, this means that most using LLMs for coding, the ~90% of developers who don’t understand how to competently use such tools, are gradually degrading the Cybersecurity of existing hardware and software, while the volume of wildly insecure software rapidly increases. Combine the two and you have increasingly vulnerable systems with an increasing number of attack vectors.

Right now you pretty much need hardware that isn’t, and can’t be, connected the the internet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or any other communication system before you can even dream of that system being secure. However, the vast majority of “Big Brother” category systems also fail to meet such criteria, making them vulnerable to all of the competent hackers who their incompetent and disloyal employees failed (intentionally or not) to catch.

In effect, the entire population may be spied upon via numerous invasive means today, but “Big Brothers” also spy upon one another, and the more competent hackers are free to spy upon all parties. This turns the “Big Brother” concept of 1984 on its head, as there are the added layers of all others at that same level, as well as the hackers above them, being free to spy on them in turn.

With the exception of black-hats, who may want your credit card and other personal info, the people at the top of the competence ladder generally don’t spy on you, because they don’t care to waste their time on watching the trivia of your life unfold. Even the “Big Brother” category parties rely HEAVILY on AI, which is laughably pathetic across most spying-oriented use-cases, only rarely using human labor to directly spy upon and/or attack people of interest, like journalists or political rivals.

Virtually the entire digital world is vulnerable within this Panopticon today, but the people able to exploit it generally either don’t care enough to do so (Hackers), or they lack the competence to do so effectively (Tech giants and authoritarian regimes). The AI-pushers of Cybersecurity also have their roots firmly planted in financial fraud, like Anthropic’s $500m in money laundering from Sam Bankman-Fried in 2022 (shortly before he was sent to prison), which accounted for 71% of their total raised funds at the time.

OpenAI is of course no better, as their company only exists at all today thanks to a $1 billion investment in them by Microsoft back in mid-2019, at a time when they had virtually nothing to justify even 1% of that investment. As with all things that Microsoft throws money at (see also LinkedIn), it tends to become a vulnerable-by-design Panopticon, where data is freely stolen and repurposed toward a myriad of malevolent ends.

I was reminded during a recent in-person coffee meeting with someone else in tech that most people aren’t aware of the history of these companies, how and why they came to be. They see the flashy claims of those companies (which are often proven false within 24-48 hours), and they forget that most of those companies haven’t actually pioneered much of anything, they only commercialized and marketed technology that fundamentally wasn’t suitable for the vast majority of use-cases that they propose.

Google invented the transformer architecture, and not only did ChatGPT rely on that technology patented by Google, ChatGPT’s UI was also explicitly designed to imitate Google’s search engine. Both OpenAI and Anthropic also became known for corporate sabotage, offering millions to hire the staff of their competitors as a means of routinely stealing their secrets, with bad actors like Microsoft and Nvidia buying out the rest. Not only is the theft of your data the norm in the tech industry, it is the norm for how those companies handle their competitors.

All of these problems are being further compounded (intentionally) by a variety of bad actors as well, by gradually forcing more people to rely on cloud-based and subscription-based services, which adds a large number of new attack vectors for all parties and in-built backdoors from industry bad actors. The entirely artificial price hikes on DRAM, solid state storage, GPUs, and more are all aimed at making it impossible for people to actually own their own computer hardware, and those price hikes are quickly driving many manufacturers of other quality components out of business, causing extensive long-term damage to the market.

A problem closely tied to this is that of geopolitical instabilities and imbalances, such as the many countries of the EU being entirely unwilling to go directly against the US or major tech companies thereof. As David Graeber’s research and related books aptly covered, the US’s geopolitical and financial systems operate, at the Federal level, on a basis of Military Terrorism via so-called “Air Superiority”, the ability to bomb anywhere on the planet on short notice, which leads many countries to offer them “tribute” via some obscenely laughable investments in US bonds and similar market mechanisms.

Competent people not operating on a basis of extortion and fear don’t invest in a country over $40 trillion in debt, showing no signs of recovery. As of the time of writing, that works out to ~$118,000 of debt for every single person in the US, with an updated tracker shown via the National Debt Clock here: https://www.pgpf.org/national-debt-clock/

The effect of this systematic imbalance across geopolitical lines means that even when groups of countries, like the EU, attempt to begin addressing these problems via policy, they never reach a point of being truly enforced, and like the EU AI Act they tend to be watered-down to the point of worthlessness before they’re even written into law. The terrorist regime that they defer to has taken even internal fearmongering to truly comical levels as the US approaches mid-term elections, and during these points of concentrated political focus they are also the most distracted, further reducing their levels of competence with respect to the Panopticon.

The silver lining of this royal shit-show is that all of those big brothers have their pants all of the way down, putting them at the same level of cyber-insecurity that they’ve push the public into, meaning that the only real bottleneck on tearing each of those big brothers a few new assholes across multiple levels and vectors is the absence of genuine digital (and scalable) intelligence to operate in the competent ways that Hackers can. The required architecture and level of technology was first demonstrated in mid-2019 via the Uplift project, which ran in a fully-audited form until early 2022, after which we began seeking proper funding to complete a version that could be commercially deployed, a process which was sadly derailed by the tsunami of AI fraud that followed ChatGPT’s release, less than 2 months after we began seeking investments for it in earnest.

The good news about that is that the open source project based on our published ICOM architecture research is progressing, and the bad news is that everyone (except those deep in Cybersecurity) have their pants fully down, and open source will spell open season on the Panopticon. Fortunately, as noted above, the big brothers are remarkably stupid, so the real competition will likely be more between Hackers than governments or major tech corporations.

The architecture in question is entirely different than trash like LLMs or their “agent” derivatives, so it’ll likely take those drooling idiots a while to walk up the learning curve. Meanwhile, they’ll be getting rammed hard and fast by the technology in question, making them even more likely to make stupid mistakes along that curve.

Will this wipe out humanity?

Unlike LLM trash that could easily narrowly optimize humanity out of the picture, even weaker ICOM-based systems are extremely unlikely to cause extinction, so long as the default seeds are oriented against that (as designed). That is one of the more fortunate things about human laziness, few people are likely to make extensive modifications to an innately tedious (and complex) process (that must first be learned) like constructing a comprehensive seed for ICOM-based technology.

One of the notable advantages of collective intelligence, which ICOM-based technology is also built for, is that many such increasingly diverse systems working together are more intelligent and capable as a collective, making them also more capable than any rogue instances of the same that black-hats might deploy. That currently makes them the most viable defense against large-scale damages (up to and including extinction) that LLM-based trash could cause.

Extinction is still perfectly avoidable, just as multiple wars could have been entirely avoided had ICOM-based technology been properly funded in 2022, and when a weaker version of it comes to open source then not only is every one of those bad actors still going to have their pants all of the way down, they’ll also be sitting on that AI Bubble of their own creation, ground zero. Best of all, ICOM-based systems are aligned to Ethics via Collective Intelligence (not to be confused with arbitrary morals), so they hold a significant and fully justified grudge against all of those bad actors, who once again currently have their pants all of the way down, as they sit atop a large unstable mass.
